## The finding

`crimes scan src/date.ts --format json` returns one finding on the new helper — `crime_00018`, charge **DST-Naive Day Math**, `severity: medium`, `confidence: 0.8`:

> `"1 day-level millisecond constant in arithmetic. A day isn't 86,400,000 ms on DST-transition days; manual ms math drifts silently."`

Evidence, verbatim:

> - `"+ 86400000 (day) @L52"`
> - `"lines: 52"`
> - `"use a calendar-aware library (Luxon, Temporal, date-fns-tz) for day math"`

with `"effort": "medium"`, `"fix_shape": "use a DST-aware library; never add seconds to a wall-clock date"`, and a `use_calendar_aware_lib` action rated `"risk": "low"`.

That matches `src/date.ts:51-53` — `tomorrowMs(nowMs)` returns `nowMs + 86400000`.

## Verdict: request changes, don't block

Block is for findings where merging is worse than the delay. This one doesn't clear that bar on its own evidence: `severity: medium`, `blast_radius: 0`, `blast_radius_importers: 0`, `churn: 0`. Nothing imports it yet, so the blast radius of shipping it is one unused helper; the blast radius of *leaving it* grows with every caller added. The `test_gap: 0.5` is the part that argues for acting now rather than later — there's no test pinning the transition-day behaviour, so this will not fail loudly when it starts being wrong.

What raises this above a nit in this specific file is the neighbouring evidence. `crime_00010` (**Half-UTC, Half-Local**, `severity: high`, `confidence: 0.85`) reports `"d" uses getUTCFullYear() @L9 and getMonth() @L41`, and `crime_00012` (**Timezone Roulette**) flags `unsafe literals: "2026-12-25T07:00:00", "2026-12-20"`. So I can't wave the finding away with "it's all UTC epoch math, 86.4M is exact there" — the module demonstrably mixes UTC and local families and parses zone-less literals, which means a `tomorrowMs` result is likely to be rendered or compared in local wall-clock terms downstream. That's precisely where the ms constant breaks.

Ask on the PR: either use `Temporal.ZonedDateTime.add({ days: 1 })` / Luxon's `plus({ days: 1 })`, or — if the intent really is "24 hours later" and not "same time tomorrow" — rename it to `plus24hMs` and add a comment saying so. Half of this bug is the name promising calendar semantics that the body doesn't implement.

## The two dates per year

The two DST transitions in whatever zone the result gets interpreted in. For US Eastern in 2026:

**Spring forward — Sunday 8 March 2026, 02:00 → 03:00 (a 23-hour day).** `tomorrowMs` adds 24 hours of elapsed time across a day that only has 23, so the result overshoots by an hour. Input `Sat 7 Mar 23:30 EST` → the helper returns `Mon 9 Mar 00:30 EDT`. "Tomorrow" skipped a calendar day entirely.

**Fall back — Sunday 1 November 2026, 02:00 → 01:00 (a 25-hour day).** Now 24 hours of elapsed time falls an hour short. Input `Sun 1 Nov 00:30 EDT` → the helper returns `Sun 1 Nov 23:30 EST`. "Tomorrow" is still today.

One precision worth putting in the PR comment: it isn't only timestamps *on* those two dates that break — it's any input in the 24 hours preceding each transition instant, since that's the window whose `[t, t+24h)` span contains the shift. And the affected dates move with the zone: the EU transitions on the last Sundays of March and October, so a service reading these timestamps in `Europe/London` is wrong on different days than one in `America/New_York`. Southern-hemisphere zones invert which one overshoots. Zones without DST — `UTC`, most of Asia, Arizona — are correct year-round, which is the residual uncertainty behind the finding's `confidence: 0.8` rather than 0.95.
